newsitem.title: MEXICO: Zapata's grandson defeated at polls in Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Zapata's grandson defeated at polls in Mexico.

text.p: The grandson of a hero of the Mexican Revolution, who had hoped for a peaceful uprising of his own at the polls, was thwarted in his bid for public office, according to official elections results released on Monday.

Emiliano Zapata Sandoval, the grandson of his namesake Emiliano Zapata, lost to the party he turned against in his bid to become mayor of Ayala, a town of 40,000 people in Morelos state, which is just south of Mexico City.

Near-final results from Sunday's voting show Hector Plasencia Ayala of the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) with 5,762 votes or 37 percent of the vote compared to Zapata Sandoval's 3,873 votes or 25 percent as candidate for the leftist Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD).

Zapata Sandoval could not be reached for comment on Monday, but in an interview with Reuters on Sunday he spoke of his disillusionment with the PRI, to which his father, another Emiliano Zapata, still belongs.
"What Mexico needs is another revolution, but with ballots not bullets," Zapata Sandoval said, denouncing what he considers PRI manipulation of poor peasants for political purposes.
Nonetheless, Zapata Sandoval's party posted big gains elsewhere in Morelos in a significant rebuke of the PRI.

"It's no longer necessary that so many people die," said Zapata Sandoval, 47, who is known simply as "Zapata's grandson" in the region, a far cry from his grandfather's nickname of "Great Leader of the South."

The first Emiliano Zapata was one of the main political-military leaders of the Mexican Revolution, which ousted longtime dictator Porfirio Diaz in 1911 and ushered in a new government under Zapata's war cry of "Land and Liberty."

Gen. Zapata embodied the revolution as the quintessential macho with a wide sombrero and moustache, a bandolier strapped across his chest. He was ambushed and killed after the revolution in 1919 by followers of de facto leader Venustiano Carranza.

His grandson the mayoral candidate bears a resemblance with his hat, moustache and broad shoulders, but without the hardware. He cast his ballot on Sunday wearing an opened-collar shirt and traditional sandals known as huaraches.

This Zapata, like many of the voters in predominantly rural Morelos, makes his living off the land, growing crops and raising animals. Like his grandfather, Zapata Sandoval says his goal is "to improve the conditions of the peasants."
